title: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
tagline: Explore a graph in rings of increasing distance — the tool for shortest paths on unweighted graphs.

intuition.analogy: Drop a stone in a pond. The ripple reaches all points one metre away before any point two metres away. BFS is that ripple — it visits everything at distance 1, then distance 2, and so on.
paragraphs: BFS explores a graph level by level using a queue. Starting from a source, it visits all immediate neighbours, then their neighbours, expanding outward in waves of equal distance.
Because it expands in order of distance, the first time BFS reaches a node is via a shortest path (in edges). That makes BFS the canonical algorithm for shortest paths on unweighted graphs and grids.
The visited set is essential: mark a node when you enqueue it (not when you dequeue) to avoid adding it twice. Each vertex and edge is processed once, giving linear time.
intuition.keyIdea: A queue processes nodes in distance order, so the first visit to any node is along a shortest (fewest-edge) path.

steps.title: Initialise
steps.detail: Put the source in a queue and mark it visited (distance 0).

steps.title: Process the queue
steps.detail: Dequeue a node, then for each unvisited neighbour, mark it visited, set its distance = current + 1, and enqueue it.

steps.title: Terminate
steps.detail: When the queue empties, every reachable node has been visited with its shortest distance recorded.

complexity.timeReason: Every vertex is enqueued once and every edge examined once.
complexity.spaceReason: The queue and visited/distance structures hold up to V vertices.

pitfalls: Marking visited at dequeue time lets duplicates pile up in the queue — mark at enqueue.
BFS gives shortest paths only for unweighted (or equal-weight) edges; use Dijkstra otherwise.
On grids, remember to bound moves and treat obstacles as non-neighbours.

dryRun.clickMoment: Distances come out grouped: all 1s, then all 2s, then 3. Node 6 is reached via 1→4→6 at distance 3 — the first arrival is automatically the shortest.

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.statement: Count connected groups of land in a grid.
problems.hint: BFS/DFS flood fill from each unvisited land cell.

approach: Scan the grid; each unvisited land cell starts a new island. Flood-fill its whole component with BFS, marking cells visited.
The number of flood-fills is the island count. O(rows·cols).

problems.title: Rotting Oranges
problems.statement: Minutes until all oranges rot, spreading to neighbours.
problems.hint: Multi-source BFS from all initially rotten oranges.

approach: All rotten oranges spread simultaneously, so this is multi-source BFS: enqueue every rotten cell at time 0.
Each BFS layer is one minute. Track fresh count; if any fresh remain after BFS, return -1, else the number of layers.

problems.title: Word Ladder
problems.statement: Shortest transformation sequence between two words.
problems.hint: BFS over words where edges connect one-letter changes.
problems.tests: BFS shortest path on an implicit graph.

approach: Each word is a node; edges connect words differing by one letter. The shortest transformation is an unweighted shortest path → BFS.
Generate neighbours by replacing each position with a-z and checking the dictionary. BFS layers count the ladder length.

problems.title: 01 Matrix
problems.statement: Distance of each cell to the nearest 0.
problems.hint: Multi-source BFS seeded with all zeros.

approach: Distance to the nearest 0 for every cell: seed a multi-source BFS with all 0-cells at distance 0.
BFS expands outward in unit steps, so the first time a 1-cell is reached gives its nearest-zero distance.
